extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, research mathematicians, and graduate students interested in mathematical practice and proof evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: A rubric for judging mathematical work (proofs, theorems, exposition) using the epistemic virtues emphasized in the philosophy of mathematical practice; intended to guide both product- and process-level evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor (contextually appropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions follow from premises through acceptable deductive steps; standards of rigor are contextual and differ across subfields and historical periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether deductive steps meet the community standards for the relevant subfield and historical moment rather than applying a single universal formal standard. Note that 'rigor pluralism' recognizes multiple legitimate models; score whether the work is rigorous for its subfield's accepted practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical explanation (explanatory power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides a 'why' in addition to a 'that' — explains why a theorem holds, not merely that it does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value proofs that illuminate reasons and mechanisms; multiple proofs for the same theorem may be produced specifically for explanatory value. Prefer arguments that make causal or structural reasons clear rather than opaque verification-only proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses methods and concepts appropriate to the disciplinary boundaries of the result (topical and geographical purity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topical purity: the proof uses only concepts present in the theorem's statement when possible. Geographical purity: avoids importing tools from distant fields (e.g., complex analysis) if a direct argument within the field exists. Purity is a virtue but can be traded off against other virtues (e.g., fruitfulness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization and diagrammatic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Employs diagrams and visual reasoning when they fulfill epistemic functions that textual/formal argument alone does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat diagrams as genuine justificatory resources; a formally correct proof that suppresses an available diagram for ideological reasons may be inferior. Assess whether visualization aids understanding, insight, or discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Contains non-obvious, non-routine ideas and genuine intellectual insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score higher if the argument requires original conceptual moves or overcomes substantial obstacles (cf. Gowers' discussion of depth). Routine or technical verifications score lower on depth even if correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses minimal apparatus and avoids unnecessary technical machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor arguments that achieve results with fewer assumptions, lemmas, or complex constructions, all else equal. Simplicity interacts with depth and explanatory power—very simple but uninformative proofs may be less valuable than slightly more complex but insightful ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontological parsimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Makes minimal commitments to existence or ontological claims beyond what is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs/theories that avoid postulating unnecessary mathematical objects. Evaluate the necessity of existence claims and whether weaker ontological assumptions would suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires minimal background knowledge from the reader to understand the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how accessible the proof is given standard background for the intended audience; proofs that demand extensive specialized machinery lower epistemic economy unless justified by other virtues (e.g., generalizability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Generates further results or opens new directions for inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value proofs or methods that lead to corollaries, generalizations, new conjectures, or techniques useful elsewhere. Fruitfulness may justify departures from purity or simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty (aesthetic appeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Possesses aesthetic qualities mathematicians recognize as 'beautiful' (symmetry, elegance, surprising simplicity, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that beauty is a genuine epistemic judgment among mathematicians (empirically attested). Use aesthetic judgments cautiously and as one among several virtues; record what features motivate the aesthetic appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of proof extends to other cases or suggests broader applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer arguments that indicate a path to more general results or that apply to families of problems; assess how directly the method transfers and whether adaptation is straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bottom-up structural analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate mathematics by detailed analysis of its actual structure rather than imposing top-down formal principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the internal structure, steps, and local reasoning moves of the proof. Avoid over-reliance on external formal criteria disconnected from the proof's practice and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situated practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize mathematicians as cognitively bounded, collaborative, reliant on testimony, and subject to negotiated community standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, take account of collaborative methods, use of informal justification, dependence on prior literature, and community norms. Process elements (how results were achieved) matter to overall assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pluralism among proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Different proofs of the same theorem can embody distinct virtues; they should not be collapsed into a single ranking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow multiple, incommensurable evaluations (e.g., one proof higher on simplicity, another on explanatory power). Use multi-dimensional scoring or narrative assessment rather than a single aggregate score where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product vs. process distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the finished mathematical product (proof/theorem) from the process that produced it; evaluate both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the product by the epistemic virtues (rigor, depth, simplicity, etc.). Judge the process by features like reasoning style, use of diagrams, collaboration, and the conjecture-and-refutation cycle. A complete evaluation reports on both aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: The process demonstrates attention to counterexamples and uses them to refine conjectures and proofs (Lakatosian practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score processes higher if they actively test conjectures against counterexamples, revise definitions, and incorporate negative evidence into theory development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveying alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The work considers alternative proofs, methods, or formulations (Avigad's suggested practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the author(s) explored or acknowledged alternative approaches and why the chosen method was preferred; surveying alternatives strengthens explanatory and justificatory claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of style to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The style, level of detail, and presentation are suited to the intended audience (Tappenden).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether exposition balances rigor, explanation, and background requirements for its target readers; a highly terse research-note style may be appropriate for experts but not for pedagogical exposition.
